text.p: A break in the drought and a concession by the European Union are helping French farmers complete grain sowings held up by brutally hard soil -- but worries remain over water needed for irrigation in the months ahead.
Too much rain too quickly could cause further delays by preventing farmers from getting into their fields.
But for now, conditions are just right for loosening the rocklike terrain which has prevented farmers sowing about half the maize crop in southern France, experts said.

"There were places where you couldn't even plough because it was too hard. Farmers will be able to prepare the ground and finish sowings fairly quickly if the right conditions persist," an official at the AGPM maize growers' association said.
Also making life easier was a concession won by France in European sowing rules, which had threatened to leave some farmers outside the deadline for sowing crops eligible for aid.
The French farm ministry said on Tuesday the EU had agreed to its request to push back the sowing deadline for maize, sorghum, soya and sunflower -- all late-planted crops -- by two weeks to May 30.
Maize, which makes up a quarter of the French grain crop, is about fully planted in the north but only half complete in the drier but more important maize regions of the south.
The AGPM official said farmers' first priority would be to replough land that had been prepared for sowing but had since been wrecked by drought and partial frost.
"Some of them will have to break up earlier ploughing tracks and big clods of earth which had become like rocks," he said.
With luck, sowings could then be finished in about two weeks, he said.
Getting an overall impression was hard because showery and stormy spells had brought rain to some farms while others still had hardly any moisture, a crop expert in central France said.
Weather service Meteo France said a wide band of rain, accompanied by hail and storms in some areas, was spreading eastwards on the tail of a previous cloud system.
But while fields were beginning to moisten, water resources were still very depleted and irrigation could be a problem as the maize harvest develops, crop experts warned.
Underground water tables are up to 50 percent below normal levels and farmers in 23 areas already face irrigation curbs. The key question is the timing of any new restrictions.

"The most vulnerable time for maize is August. So the nearer to August the restrictions come the worse it is," the AGPM official said. For now, however, it was impossible to be either optimistic or pessimistic about the crop.
About 45 percent of French maize grown for commercial grain use, about 1.72 million hectares, is irrigated.

Last year's average national yield hit a record 8.4 tonnes a hectare lifting production to a record near 14.5 million tonnes. A more normal yield is between 7.8 and 8.0 tonnes, the AGPM official said, pointing to a harvest of 13.4 to 13.7 million tonnes based on unchanged sowing areas.
